newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Squalor and misery reign at Albanian hospital.
newsitem.headline: Squalor and misery reign at Albanian hospital.

text.p: Blood soaked bandages and used syringes litter the garden of southern Albania's largest hospital, while inside patients lie on filthy sheets in ramshackle wards.
To go into the general hospital at this Adriatic port is to enter a time warp, isolated from modern medical advances and devoid of basic hygiene care.

"Of course there is a problem here, how could anyone be happy with these conditions?" said head surgeon Kristaq Bisholla. "We repeatedly ask for equipment but receive virtually nothing from the state," he added.
With the Albanian government desperately short of cash, the doctors hope western governments will come to their rescue.
"We don't need instruments made in 1996. Things produced in 1980 would still be modern for us," said Zija Saliu, the hospital's orthopedic specialist.

Vlore's crumbling hospital, which has not seen a fresh coat of paint since it was built in the 1960s, was swamped earlier this week with people injured in violent clashes sparked by the collapse of a local pyramid fund.
Staff struggled to cope with the influx and were forced to cram two people to a bed in the casuality department.

A pair of orderlies carried dirty dressings out to a barren patch of land by the back of the morgue, and tossed the rubbish onto the ground. One of the two women tried to wipe smears of blood off a plastic sheet with her shoe.
Cats and dogs roamed the wasteland and plastic syringes crackled underfoot on the short walk back to the main doorway.

"We only started using plastic syringes this year and don't yet have an incinerator to get rid of them. Maybe we'll build one later this year, but funds are very low," said Servet Kojdheli, the regional director of the hospital.
In the meantime the fluid-filled syringes are simply tossed out of the doors where small children play with them.
The Vlore hospital serves some 200,000 people from the surrounding regions and is one of the largest medical centres outside the Albanian capital Tirana.
Morale among the staff is low, with many of the doctors left penniless by the failure of the investment funds and struggling to make ends meet on paltry wages.
"I work six days a week and earn just $62 a month," said Alfred Mucho, one of the hospital's 12-strong team of surgeons. "Nowhere else in Europe do doctors get so badly paid."
Patients sleep in cramped, unheated wards, lit by naked light bulbs and with chunks of masonry falling off the walls.
Doctors say they have received some medical supplies from the outside world, but the equipment often arrives unannounced and does not serve their purposes.

A senior official at an international agency based in Tirana, who declined to be named, agreed that much of the aid sent to Europe's poorest nation was of little use, saying that some of it arrived without explanation and was never used.
But she said there was also a lack of initative and understanding on the part of many Albanian medical staff.
"We went to one children's unit in a northern hospital and asked what the staff needed. They asked for a television, but the children didn't even have clothes," she said.
